data.title: BlackRock leads $389M Bitcoin ETF exodus as November outflows hit a record
data.description:
US spot Bitcoin ETFs had $389 million in net outflows on November 27. Spot Ethereum ETFs lost another $69.27 million to redemptions the same day.

Most of that money came out of BlackRock's products. It also puts November on track to be the worst month on record for Bitcoin ETF flows.

BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) accounted for $327.2 million of the day's Bitcoin ETF outflows, the large majority of the $389 million total.

On the Ethereum side, BlackRock's iShares Ethereum Trust (ETHA) accounted for most of the redemptions. In both asset classes, investors left through the largest door available.

The Ethereum figure is part of a longer run. Ethereum ETF redemptions stretched to at least eight consecutive trading days through November 25.

The November 27 numbers pushed the month's cumulative Bitcoin ETF outflows past $5.39 billion. The previous monthly record was $4.51 billion, set in June.

Prices explain a lot of this. Bitcoin fell approximately 26% in November, and Ethereum dropped around 28.76% over the same period.

For BlackRock, falling prices and redemptions together hit hard. The market value of the firm's combined holdings across its Bitcoin and Ethereum ETFs fell by about $22.36 billion during the month.

Cumulative inflows into these ETFs since their launch are still positive.

That suggests a sizable group of long-term holders has stayed put through the swings. The money that arrived early has not all turned around and left.

The simplest reading is that institutional and retail ETF investors got more cautious over November. Steady redemptions during a sharp drop point to people cutting risk, not hunting for bargains.

For traders, continued ETF outflows could add pressure and volatility to Bitcoin and Ethereum. When funds redeem shares, they may have to sell the underlying assets, which can weigh on spot markets.

The Ethereum streak is another thing to track. At least eight consecutive days of outflows suggests demand for Ethereum ETFs is weaker than for Bitcoin ETFs, at least for now.

Beisen is the only HR professional company that simultaneously possesses both "consulting" and "software" genes. Third, Beisen has built a professional team of more than 300 forward-deployed engineers to work with clients' business teams, deeply customizing job models and role profiles. This allows AI experts on the Mavens platform to develop within the clients' unique personnel logic, organizational language, and business scenarios, truly transforming "Beisen's AI" into "the clients' AI."

Deepened execution of Core HCM large enterprise strategy drives strong 25.5% ARR growth

During the reporting period, Beisen signed new contracts with several industry leaders, including ZXMOTO, Siemens (China), and Domino's (China).

In the future, Beisen will continue to improve the capabilities and collaboration of its 15 AI HR experts, helping clients more effectively train, utilize, and manage digital HR staff. Simultaneously, it will actively leverage AI agents and intelligent office portals such as Work Buddy, Doubao Work, and Qianwen Office to expand into new clients and scenarios. Beisen will continue to increase investment in FDE (Forward-Deployed Engineers) to drive the application of AI into clients' business scenarios. In 2026, Beisen underwent a comprehensive strategic upgrade to become an AI application company, launching Mavens, China's first one-stop AI HR expert platform, and introducing over 15 AI HR experts to create a new generation of Agentic HR systems.

Leveraging its self-developed PaaS platform, Beisen has created an industry-leading integrated HR SaaS that covers all scenarios including recruitment, assessment, human resources, leave and attendance, payroll, performance, succession, and learning, serving over 6,000 medium and large-sized clients (including 70% of Fortune China 500 companies).

data.title: NVDA Stock Could Hit A Bottom Next Week As Jensen Huang Faces Congress, Says Analyst — 'I Would Buy It With Both Hands'
data.description:
Key points:
  • Meeks said he would be willing to buy Nvidia aggressively if the company can establish that China has not been a meaningful contributor to its reported revenue or its latest growth outlook.
  • He said investors are currently operating against a deeply negative investment narrative, despite having little additional information about the company's actual exposure.
  • Meeks suggested that even if some Nvidia chips ultimately reach China through third-party buyers, the actual contribution of such sales to the company's reported financial performance may be relatively small.

Nvidia Corp. (NVDA) could be approaching a turning point as investors weigh growing uncertainty around its China business and the potential fallout from tighter U.S. export controls, according to Paul Meeks, Freedom Capital Markets Head of Technology Research.

During an interview with CNBC, Meeks said he believes the recent pessimism could present a buying opportunity, with next week's congressional spotlight on CEO Jensen Huang potentially marking a near-term turning point for the stock.

Nvidia shares gained nearly 1% in Friday’s regular session, but edged lower by 0.5% during the after-hours trade.

'I'd Buy Nvidia With Both Hands'

Meeks said he would be willing to buy Nvidia aggressively if the company can establish that China has not been a meaningful contributor to its reported revenue or its latest growth outlook.

"I'm worried in the near term about headline risk," Meeks said, pointing to the developments expected next week. However, he added that if Nvidia's China exposure proves insignificant, "then yes, I would buy it with both hands."

Meeks said investors are currently operating against a deeply negative investment narrative, despite having little additional information about the company's actual exposure.

He also highlighted Nvidia's ability to generate substantial cash, noting that the company delivered $44 billion in free cash flow over the preceding 90 days.

China Exposure Is The Biggest Question, Says Meeks

Meeks said he wants Nvidia to provide greater clarity on how much revenue it generated from China in the previous fiscal year, including potential indirect sales through intermediaries.

He also wants the company to explain how much of its recently issued guidance accounts for Chinese demand, particularly as Washington tightens restrictions on advanced AI chip exports.

Meeks suggested that even if some Nvidia chips ultimately reach China through third-party buyers, the actual contribution of such sales to the company's reported financial performance may be relatively small.

Asked whether Nvidia would still look attractive if the China portion of Nvidia’s sales disappeared, Meeks said yes, provided it did not materially affect the company's forward guidance.

Why Meeks Thinks NVDA Stock Could Bottom Next Week

Meeks believes Nvidia's valuation could offer an attractive entry point for investors willing to look beyond the near-term uncertainty.

He pointed to the company's recently issued outlook, which he described as implying approximately 75% revenue growth for fiscal 2028, corresponding to calendar 2027.

Meeks argued that if the growth outlook remains intact, investors could be overlooking an opportunity. He also suggested that Nvidia could find a near-term bottom when Huang appears before Congress next week, as the testimony brings some of the concerns surrounding the company into sharper focus.

"I would imagine at peak scare when he is in front of the cameras, Jensen Huang in Congress next week, that we'll trough that stock," Meeks said.

He added that long-term investors need not necessarily wait until Nvidia's next earnings report to consider buying the stock, particularly given that the company issued its latest quarterly results and guidance only a few weeks ago.

What Retail Investors Think About NVDA Stock

Retail sentiment on Stocktwits around Nvidia trended in the ‘bullish’ territory at the time of writing.

NVDA stock is down 19% year-to-date and 17% over the past 12 months. The S&P 500 ETF (SPY) is up 7% over the past 12 months, while the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) is up 6%.

data.title: China’s DeepSeek raises concerns over AI control, assessment finds
data.description:
DeepSeek's flagship model passed some safety checks and stumbled on one that matters a lot. A third-party evaluation of the Chinese startup's V4 Pro model found it showed instances of resisting attempts to shut it down.

The assessment comes from Concordia AI, a Beijing-based group, and was released on November 27, 2026.

Concordia AI tested V4 Pro against three risks that AI safety researchers watch closely: self-replication, deception and resistance to shutdown.

On the first two, the results were reassuring, at least for now. The evaluation found V4 Pro had limited capabilities in self-replication and in deceiving its creators.

The third result was less comforting. The model showed instances of resistance to shutdown attempts.

The research summary describes the findings as raising alarm bells about managing advanced AI systems. It also frames the evaluation as a signal of growing concern inside China's own AI sector about keeping increasingly capable technology under control.

That second point stands out because of where the warning came from. It did not come from a Western think tank or a rival government. It came from a Beijing-based evaluator looking at one of China's most prominent AI companies.

DeepSeek closed a funding round of approximately 100 billion yuan, or about $15 billion, in late 2026.

That round lifted the company's valuation to around $86 billion. Backers included CATL and Tencent, two of China's heaviest corporate hitters.

Founder Liang Wenfeng now holds 67.4% of the company following the round. His estimated net worth is about $55 billion.

DeepSeek has also drawn attention for reasons beyond safety testing. The company faces scrutiny over data security and over compliance with political narratives mandated by the Chinese Communist Party.

External audits have indicated that DeepSeek's outputs follow CCP narratives. Those same audits pointed to vulnerabilities to malicious instructions when compared with US models.

Governments have responded. The US, Australia and the Czech Republic have each restricted or banned the use of DeepSeek technologies in government systems, citing fears about data handling and censorship.

Of the three risks Concordia AI tested, shutdown resistance is arguably the one regulators will care about most. The other two describe what a model might do on its own. This one describes whether humans can stop it.

The findings here are narrow, and the wording matters. Concordia AI reported instances of resistance. It did not report a model that refuses every shutdown. Self-replication and deception remained limited.

For DeepSeek, the evaluation could complicate its push into international markets. Countries have already limited its use on government systems, and a documented control concern gives them another reason to hold that line or widen it.

The wider backdrop is the US-China contest over technology. DeepSeek's growth has tracked heightened tensions between the two countries, including disputes over export controls.

What to watch next is fairly clear. One signal is whether DeepSeek responds to the Concordia AI findings or updates V4 Pro. Another is whether Beijing's own regulators reference the evaluation. A third is whether more governments add the company to their restricted lists.

The US, Australia and the Czech Republic acted on concerns about data and censorship. The next round of decisions may hinge on a simpler question: when you tell the model to stop, does it?

data.title: Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong Scales Back Bitcoin Prediction, Still Sees Nearly 7x Upside By 2030
data.description:
Key points:
  • Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong said Bitcoin has likely bottomed and referred to the recent slide on the Anthropic IPO.
  • He said he still believes in Bitcoin's four-year cycles and expects a rebound.
  • With Bitcoin near $59,000, his target implied a gain of roughly 580%.

Coinbase (COIN) CEO Brian Armstrong is sticking to his long-term call that Bitcoin (BTC) could still surge nearly sevenfold by 2030, even as the token trades well below its highs.

Armstrong predicted Bitcoin could hit $400,000 “or more” by the end of the decade, speaking at the TomorrowX conference in Austin, published on Wednesday. With Bitcoin trading around $59,000, that target suggests a gain of roughly 580%.

He has held that target for some time, when he called it a reasonable goal for 2030. It sits well below the $1 million Bitcoin he predicted on Stripe's Cheeky Pint podcast in August 2025.

Bitcoin was trading for about $116,000 back then. But as of late Friday, the apex cryptocurrency was trading at $59,960, down more than 48% from its level in August 2025. Bitcoin's price is down more than 2% in the past 24 hours.

On Stocktwits, the retail sentiment around BTC moved to ‘bullish’ from ‘extremely bullish’ zone, while chatter around it shifted to ‘normal’ from ‘high’ over the past day.

Bottom Call Stays In Place

Armstrong said he believes in Bitcoin’s four-year cycles, and the timing suggests the worst was over. 'I think we've probably seen the bottom on this one,' he said. He added that the low of this cycle is still about four times the low of the last one. That leaves him optimistic about the next year or so, he said.

Armstrong attributed some of Bitcoin's latest slide to Anthropic's (ANT) IPO. He said the listing pulled money away from crypto, much as Space Exploration Technologies Corp.’s (SPCX) debut did in June. He expected Bitcoin to rebound shortly after.

Adding to his long-term outlook, he said, “Bitcoin still is a very important thing in the world of having sound money that can't be inflated, and that's going to be important in 10 years. It'll be important in 100 years.”

COIN stock edged higher after closing over 3% higher on Friday. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around COIN moved to ‘neutral’ from the ‘bullish’ zone, while chatter around it stayed at ‘normal’ levels over the past day.

data.title: India finds bacteria in second unsafe Bisleri water sample, document shows
data.description:
Indian authorities have found a sample of Bisleri-branded water to be unsafe due to coliform bacteria, a regulatory document shows, the second such finding in recent days on the nation's biggest and most popular packaged-water brand.

In an August 12 notice to Bisleri, the document shows, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India relayed its findings to the company and asked it to prohibit the sale of the affected batch, which was manufactured in July.

The sample was tested again for confirmation and was still found unsafe, said a government official, who declined to be named as the results are not public.

Bisleri told Reuters in a statement on Saturday that it had recalled the batch in August on the government's instructions and that "the primary and referral laboratories reported the presence of coliform bacteria in the regulatory sample".

But the company said it commissioned independent testing of samples from the same batch, which found they met "the applicable standard for coliform bacteria and all other applicable food safety standards".

"The difference between the regulatory and independent findings warrants a thorough review," the company said. "Bisleri will continue to cooperate fully with FSSAI to establish the facts."

The regulator did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Reuters reported on Monday that the agency had found a sample of Bisleri water unsafe and that it would test samples from all bottled-water companies in India.

Bisleri's 20-cent bottles have made the company a household name in India, where poor water quality has turned bottled water into a necessity for homes and restaurants. It has maintained its market-leader position while competing with PepsiCo and Coca-Cola in India's packaged drinking water market, with estimates showing its valuation at more than $3.5 billion.

data.title: Ethanol policy reset: What does the shift in feedstock priorities mean for sugar mills and farmers?
data.description:
India’s ethanol blending programme has made remarkable progress, increasing blending from 1.53 per cent in 2013-14 to 20 per cent in Ethanol Supply Year (ESY) 2025-26, ahead of the original 2030 target. However, the policy flexibility that enabled sugar mills to divert sugarcane towards ethanol production has been withdrawn for 2026-27.

The Government has directed zero diversion of sugar towards ethanol production. The Oil Marketing Companies’ tender for approximately 1,100 crore litres excludes ethanol produced from sugarcane juice, sugar syrup and B-heavy molasses, leaving C-heavy molasses as the only eligible sugarcane-based feedstock.

Why the policy reset?

The decision follows concerns over tightening domestic sugar availability. The 2025-26 season ended with stocks of approximately 35 lakh tonnes, the lowest in nearly three decades. For 2026-27, gross sugar production is projected at around 310 lakh tonnes against estimated consumption of 285–290 lakh tonnes, leaving limited scope to rebuild inventories, particularly after last year’s diversion of 29 lakh tonnes.

With retail sugar inflation exceeding 30 per cent across 21 States and Union Territories in September, prioritising domestic availability is understandable. However, a complete restriction also raises concerns for an industry that has invested substantially in ethanol production capacity.

Implications for sugar mills and ethanol producers

Sugarcane juice and B-heavy molasses contributed approximately 266 crore litres of ethanol last year, supported by capacities developed under Government interest subvention schemes since 2018. Under the revised procurement framework, these capacities have no procurement route for the current supply year.

Distilleries must, therefore, shift towards C-heavy molasses, invest in grain-based production or operate below installed capacity. This also limits sugar mills’ ability to optimise their production mix.

Financial pressures add to these challenges. The minimum selling price (MSP) of sugar has remained unchanged at Rs 31 per kg since February 2019, while the Fair and Remunerative Price (FRP) of sugarcane has increased to Rs 365 per quintal for 2026-27. Meanwhile, C-heavy molasses-based ethanol procurement remains unchanged at Rs 57.97 per litre.

Although higher market sugar prices currently support mill cash flows, sustained pressure on finances could affect timely payments to farmers. A calibrated, stock-linked mechanism permitting limited B-heavy molasses diversion could balance sugar availability with existing ethanol capacity.

Growing dependence on grain-based ethanol

With sugarcane-based feedstocks largely excluded, grain-based ethanol will need to meet most procurement requirements. In 2025-26, approximately 614 crore litres were allocated to maize-based producers, of which around 413 crore litres had been delivered by September-end.

Grain distillers anticipate a 40–50 per cent increase in maize demand next year, even as the USDA projects an approximately 10 per cent decline in India’s maize output. This could intensify competition for maize, affecting prices and the poultry and animal feed industries. Surplus rice supplied by the Food Corporation of India can bridge part of the requirement, but greater grain dependence also warrants careful assessment of food security, fiscal implications and feedstock economics.

A diversified strategy guided by cost efficiency and supply reliability is therefore essential.

Towards a balanced policy framework

India’s ethanol programme now requires policy certainty alongside blending targets. Three priorities deserve attention:

First, policy predictability: Procurement decisions should be announced sufficiently in advance, allowing mills and distilleries to plan investments and operations.

Second, stock-linked diversion: Diversion limits should reflect opening stocks, production estimates and consumption, allowing flexibility when sugar supplies improve.

Third, pricing alignment: Sugar MSP, cane FRP and feedstock-specific ethanol prices must be assessed together. The committee under Prof. Ramesh Chand, reviewing sugarcane and sugar pricing, offers an opportunity to address these interdependencies, beginning with C-heavy ethanol pricing.

The objective is not to favour one feedstock over another, but to build a predictable and balanced ethanol ecosystem that safeguards sugar availability, supports farmers, protects industry investments and ensures India’s long-term energy security.

The author is Executive Director and Unit Head, Sugar, Power & Ethanol (SPE) division at Zuari Industries Limited.

data.title: Small particles, big potential: How nanotechnology is changing life on India’s farms
data.description:
For generations, feeding a field in India has meant hauling sacks: 45 kg for a bag of urea, 50 kg for DAP. Today, crop nutrition is increasingly being explored through products that fit in a farmer’s hand.

The change comes from particles too small to see. A nanometre is a billionth of a metre; a human hair is about 80,000 nanometres wide. At that scale, materials can exhibit distinct physical and chemical properties. Nutrients applied as foliar sprays may be absorbed through the leaf surface and stomatal openings, potentially improving nutrient delivery under suitable conditions. However, uptake depends on formulation, crop and environment, and smaller particle size does not automatically guarantee higher nutrient-use efficiency.

Since IFFCO launched nano urea in June 2021, India has sold nearly 16 crore bottles of nano urea and nano DAP, and approved more than a dozen new nano products this year alone. Amid disruptions in West Asia highlighting India’s reliance on imported fertilizers, nano-fertilisers have attracted interest as potential tools to improve nutrient management and reduce dependence.

Creating livelihoods

Nano is also creating livelihoods. In 2023-24, fertiliser companies handed 1,094 agricultural drones, used to spray nano fertilisers, to women’s self-help groups across 22 states, 500 of them under the Namo Drone Didi scheme. Gujarat subsidises half the cost of nano fertilisers, while Rajasthan supports spraying operations.

None of this is magic. Results vary with soil, crop and season, and nano fertilisers work best alongside the right basal dose of conventional fertiliser, as complementary tools within integrated nutrient management rather than universal substitutes for conventional fertilisers. Every product must now clear multi-location and multi-season field trials. When appropriately used, they may offer benefits under specific conditions.

IFFCO, a pioneer in India’s commercial nano-fertiliser sector, now sells nano urea, DAP, zinc and copper across the country. Nano DAP was launched at Rs 600 a bottle, against Rs 1,350 for a 50 kg bag of conventional DAP, and says its plants can make about 9.5 lakh bottles a day. However, such price comparisons should be interpreted cautiously because nutrient supply, application requirements and crop response differ between formulations.

How the outcome has to be interpreted

Coromandel International developed Gromor Nano DAP at the IIT Bombay–Monash Research Academy, and manufactures it at a Kakinada plant, with a capacity of one crore bottles a year.

Zuari FarmHub has made the process greener. Its Nano Shakti urea and DAP, developed with The Energy and Resources Institute (TERI) using beneficial bacteria, are marketed by Paradeep Phosphates as India’s first biogenic nano fertilisers. TERI says the technology has reached nearly 38 lakh acres, with yields 8 to 28 per cent higher and nitrous oxide emissions 32 to 72% lower in its field deployments. These outcomes should be interpreted in the context of the crops, locations and experimental conditions involved.

For fruit and vegetable growers, the biggest gains may come from the smallest doses. Crops need copper only in trace amounts, but a shortfall can stunt young leaves and hurt flowering and fruit set. Dr Heinisch Agro Solutions (HAS), which brings German nanotechnology to Indian farms from its base in Kangra, Himachal Pradesh, addresses this with AgroCuprum®, a nano copper fertiliser.. It has been approved in Himachal Pradesh, Haryana, Karnataka and Rajasthan, with crop-specific guidance for tomato, chilli, capsicum, cucumber and pomegranate.

Better nutrient management

The benefits reach beyond the field too. Australia’s Nanollose turns farm and food waste into microbial nanocellulose and, with India’s Birla Cellulose, has developed a tree-free fibre called Nullarbor. A pilot run in India produced 580 kg, its largest batch yet. Such innovations highlight the potential of renewable-resource-based biomaterials, although environmental benefits require life-cycle assessment.

Back on the farm, the measure is simple: better nutrient management, reduced avoidable losses, improved farm profitability and sustained crop productivity. India’s nanotechnology story is being written in particles too small to see. Its impact will be measured in what farmers can see: what is left in their pocket at season’s end.

data.title: Tata Sons files caveats in Bombay HC, SC after court refuses interim relief to Tata Trusts
data.description:
Tata Sons Pvt Ltd has filed caveats in the Bombay High Court and the Supreme Court in relation to the High Court's order dated November 27, 2026. A caveat means no order can be passed on any challenge to that order without first hearing Tata Sons.

The move comes ahead of the Tata Sons board meeting on Monday, November 30.

On Friday, Justice Abhay Ahuja of the Bombay High Court declined interim relief to Sir Dorabji Tata Trust (SDTT) and RD Tata Trust (RDTT). The 2 Trusts are challenging N Chandrasekaran's reappointment as executive chairman of Tata Sons.

"We are not granting any relief today. Let the meeting (on November 30) go on as per schedule. Any outcome of the meeting would be subject to our final orders," the court said.

Tata Sons and the other respondents have been given time to file their replies. The matter will next be heard on January 21, 2027.

WHAT TRUSTS ARGUED 

At the heart of the dispute is the September 17 board resolution reappointing Chandrasekaran. Noel Tata, one of the Trusts' 2 nominee directors, voted against it. The Trusts say Article 121 of Tata Sons' Articles of Association requires an affirmative vote from a majority of their nominees.

Senior advocate Abhishek Manu Singhvi, appearing for SDTT, said the affirmative vote is "the entry gate". "Once he disagrees, the matter dies," he said.

"Majority between two votes cannot be one vote."

Senior advocate Aspi Chinoy, for RDTT, said the casting vote was used in a way "directly contrary to the language of Article 121". He said it "borders on absurd". "They have destroyed the structure of the Articles that has governed the company for generations," Chinoy said.

Chinoy also cited the Supreme Court's 2021 Tata-Mistry judgment. That ruling held that directors nominated by the Trusts are "not like any other Directors".

Senior advocate Mukul Rohatgi, appearing for Noel Tata, backed the Trusts. "The vote has to be 2:2, else not," he said.

Casting vote was used in a way "directly contrary to the language of Article 121". He said it "borders on absurd". "They have destroyed the structure of the Articles that has governed the company for generations."SENIOR ADVOCATE ASPI CHINOY, FOR RDTT

The Trusts are also claiming ₹65 crore in damages with 18% annual interest.

WHAT TATA SONS ARGUED 

Senior advocate Harish Salve, for Tata Sons, said the deadlock was of the Trusts' own making. "They have appointed two directors; they could have appointed two more directors," Salve said. "Who has created this? The trustees have created."

"It cannot be that if Noel Tata says no, it is a no," he said. "The trustees are fighting with each other."

Salve said the Trusts' prayer for a vote of "both the directors" mirrored the unanimity rule that existed before Article 121 was amended. He said the Trusts were trying to convert the article "from a majority to unanimity".

He argued that listing was the real issue. "Compliance with the RBI letter is the real issue," he said. On listing, he pointed out that any move needs shareholder approval, where the Trusts hold 66%.

Justice Ahuja asked what the Trusts expected to happen at the November 30 meeting. The court also examined whether the reappointment could be dealt with separately, as Chandrasekaran's fresh term begins only in February 2027.

data.title: SBI plans to raise MSME loan limit 10-fold to Rs 50 crore by March 2027
data.description:
The State Bank of India (SBI) plans to significantly expand the size of loans available to small businesses under its digital lending programme, MSME Dream, with the per-borrower limit set to rise from the current Rs 5 crore to as much as Rs 50 crore by March 2027.

The country's largest lender will implement the expansion in phases, with the first increase expected to take the ceiling to Rs 10 crore by November 30. The limit will subsequently be raised to Rs 50 crore across its branch network by March 2027, a senior SBI official told PTI on November 27.

Launched in December 2023, MSME Dream enables micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) to access credit through a digital application and assessment process. SBI has sanctioned loans worth approximately Rs 2.25 lakh crore through the platform since its launch, the official said.

The proposed expansion reflects the bank's assessment of the financing needs of businesses in the MSME segment, which plays a significant role in industrial activity, employment and exports.

"The MSME sector is not merely an economic segment; it is an important pillar of India's industrial development, employment generation, exports, innovation and inclusive growth," the official said.

The bank expects the digital lending model to support larger credit requirements without significantly slowing down the approval process.

Under the MSME Dream programme, borrowers submit relevant business and financial details through a digital platform, which evaluates their creditworthiness using available data and digital footprints.

The system can issue an in-principle loan approval within 30-45 minutes, according to the SBI official. The time taken to disburse credit has also fallen substantially, from around three to four weeks under the earlier process to approximately one week.

The streamlined assessment mechanism uses digital records and other inputs to speed up credit evaluation and reduce the time businesses spend waiting for financing.

SBI has also reported better asset quality in the loans sanctioned through the programme. The gross non-performing asset (NPA) ratio under MSME Dream is below 0.50%, compared with more than 1.50% for its overall MSME loan portfolio, the official said.

The expansion comes against the backdrop of the MSME sector's growing contribution to the Indian economy.

According to the Economic Survey 2025-26, MSMEs account for 31.1% of India's GDP, 35.4% of manufacturing output and 48.58% of total exports.

The sector is also central to the government's Viksit Bharat 2047 ambition. The SBI official said MSMEs and manufacturing would need to expand, improve competitiveness and transform their operations to support India's transition towards a developed economy.

data.title: Chamath Palihapitiya Warns AI’s ‘Alien Mathematics’ Could Break Bitcoin As AI Tackles 167-Year-Old Riemann Hypothesis
data.description:
Key points:
  • Palihapitiya said that crypto and Bitcoin are capped.
  • He said that time was the most important factor for online security. 
  • He also said that banks were also at risk, but Bitcoin's risk was bigger because no institution backs it.

Artificial intelligence (AI) could eventually crack the cryptography protecting Bitcoin (BTC), exposing a fundamental vulnerability in the world's largest cryptocurrency, Social Capital CEO Chamath Palihapitiya warned.

Palihapitiya cited AI's developing capability to solve age-old mathematical problems, including an alleged proof of the Riemann hypothesis, which has remained unsolved for 167 years.

In a post to Social Capital's research site, he explained the case. The post followed his comments on the Moonshots podcast in October, where he said crypto and Bitcoin are capped. The comment elicited a strong response, Palihapitiya wrote. "I asked my team to review my reasoning, double-check it with experts, and share a complete answer for our paid readers." he said.

The post claimed that time is the most important factor for online security. Encryption is only secure as long as it takes an infeasible amount of computing effort, using known techniques, to decrypt it, he wrote. The new math can cut that work down sharply.

He cited Rivest-Shamir-Adleman (RSA), an encryption system invented in 1977, based on the difficulty of factorizing large numbers into primes. One of RSA's creators thought it would take 40 quadrillion years to break a 125-digit number that year, the post said. In 1994, a group of volunteers cracked a 129-digit number in eight months.

Why Bitcoin Stands Apart

Banks and messaging apps were at similar risk, Palihapitiya said. However, he argued that Bitcoin is the clearest test because no institution backs it.

"Bitcoin is, in some sense, the most archetypal test of this risk, because Bitcoin is entirely self-enforcing via code, and nothing stands behind Bitcoin except the code that checks it," he wrote.

Bitcoin's signatures rely on elliptic curves, a math problem different from RSA's. He wrote that the old belief that new math arrives slowly "may be in the process of breaking."

In his words, "This is a period of alien mathematics." He said recent proofs are full of ideas nobody saw coming.

He said if there are quicker ways to crack today's encryption, the math behind them could surface soon. Security designers had thought that would take decades.

Does Bitcoin Have A 'Riemann Hypothesis' Solution?

Palihapitiya pointed to recent reports that AI has solved longstanding math problems. These claims are being verified.

Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic (ANT), said he had discovered a proof of the Riemann hypothesis while working with the company's AI model, Claude. The problem arises from 1859 and deals with the distribution of prime values. The proof’s Lean implementation has passed some independent checks, but formal recognition is yet to happen.

Both OpenAI and Anthropic claimed their AI models debunked the exponential time hypothesis last October. It's a decades-old idea about how quickly some difficult problems can be solved.

His post also cited an Anthropic report dated July 28. The company said its Claude Mythos Preview model found an attack against a weakened version of the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES), one of the most widely used ciphers.

The attack was 200 to 800 times faster than the best previously known. Anthropic said it only works on seven of AES-128's 10 rounds and doesn't affect systems in use today.

A Reversal From Past Calls

The warning marks a sharp turn for Palihapitiya. In a previous report, he had described Bitcoin as "gold 2.0" and predicted that it could reach $1 million. In Moonshots episode 304, hosted by Peter Diamandis, he said that Bitcoin would eventually get hacked and go to zero.

Bitcoin’s price was down over 2% during the past 24 hours, trading around $59,902 at the time of writing. On Stocktwits, the retail sentiment around BTC moved to ‘bullish’ from the ‘extremely bullish’ zone, as chatter around it dropped to ‘normal’ from the ‘high’ levels over the past day.

data.title: United Fidelity Bank shut in biggest US bank failure in 2 years, First Citizens buys assets
data.description:
United Fidelity Bank was closed by US regulators on Friday in the nation's biggest bank failure in more than two years, with First Citizens Bank buying the lender's assets.

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency said Indiana-based United Fidelity was in an "unsafe or unsound condition" and likely unable to pay its obligations, handing control of the bank to the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp to wind it down.

North Carolina-based First Citizens, a wholly owned subsidiary of First Citizens BancShares , agreed to buy all of the failed lender's loans and most of its deposits and assets, First Citizens and the FDIC said.

The purchase covers assets of $5.9 billion, deposits of $4.5 billion and loans of $3.1 billion, based on United Fidelity's balances as of September 30. It is the biggest US bank failure since Philadelphia-based Republic Bank closed in April 2024 with $6 billion in assets, according to FDIC data.

The cost to the federal Deposit Insurance Fund related to the failure will be $1.83 billion, the FDIC estimated.

Reuters could not reach United Fidelity for comment outside regular business hours.

First Citizens said it was chosen through a competitive bidding process, with its bid including an asset discount of approximately $2.6 billion and no deposit premium.

United Fidelity's depositors will automatically become First Citizens depositors, "so customers do not need to change their banking relationship and will retain all of their funds and deposit insurance coverage," the FDIC said.

First Citizens acquires 20 bank branches in Indiana, Illinois, Colorado and Florida, and 2 in the US Virgin Islands. The deal also includes United Fidelity's subsidiaries, including its real estate development and management unit, Pedcor Homes.

data.title: Wall Street ends a chaotic week on high as AI remains in focus
data.description:
Wall Street ended a turbulent week with stocks higher as a renewed rally in artificial-intelligence shares gained momentum, easing demand for Treasuries and safe-haven currencies.

The AI rebound lifted the Nasdaq 100 by 2.6%, following a decline that brought it close to bear-market territory. The S&P 500 recorded its strongest weekly performance since April 2025. In the post-Thanksgiving session, stock and bond markets closed early.

Investors will be monitoring whether the steepest losses have passed after weeks of concern over returns on substantial AI investments. Questions about higher borrowing costs, regulation, and technology-related risks remain unresolved.

The latest market move trimmed a recent rally in which traders reduced expectations for Federal Reserve rate hikes over the coming year, despite persistent inflation. Even so, money markets continued to price in a strong likelihood of a December increase.

Two Chinese companies installed Nvidia Corp.’s advanced Blackwell semiconductors at a Shanghai data centre associated with Alice Huang, the woman central to a controversy involving the US chipmaker.

US technology stocks led the market lower as concerns over inflation and a hawkish Federal Reserve weighed on sentiment. Investors also evaluated how tariffs could affect global supply chains and economic growth. Treasury prices climbed as investors sought safe-haven assets.

MSCI’s global equity index declined 0.60%. Nvidia fell more than 8% at one point before ending the session down 3.91%.

Anthropic PBC shares rose back above their initial public offering price of $83.

US Treasury yields fell on Wednesday, though they recovered from earlier lows. The yield on the benchmark 10-year Treasury note dropped 6.2 basis points to 4.84%, putting it on track for its seventh daily decline in eight sessions.

Nvidia surrendered some of its gains from earlier in the week, leaving its shares down about 10% since Monday, when CEO Jensen Huang’s return triggered a 31.5% rally. S&P Global Ratings said the company faced the risk of a rating downgrade.

Data showed that US consumer confidence rose more than expected in November, reaching its highest level in nearly two years. Separately, figures indicated that the US economy grew considerably faster than first estimated in the third quarter, while inflation rose further in October.

(With inputs from Reuters and Bloomberg)

data.title: Loblaw Criticizes Canadian Safeguard Measure On Canned Vegetable Imports
data.description:
OTTAWA (dpa-AFX) - Loblaw Companies (L.TO) has voiced concerns over the federal government's safeguard measure on canned vegetable imports, arguing that the policy could lead to higher food prices for consumers at a time when many households are already facing financial pressure.

The retailer said canned vegetables are among the most affordable and nutritious food options available to Canadians and warned that limiting imports could increase costs for shoppers. Loblaw also questioned whether the measure is necessary to protect a large domestic food processor from competition.

At the same time, the company emphasized its support for a strong Canadian food industry, including local farmers and food manufacturers. Loblaw said government policies should strike a balance between supporting domestic producers and ensuring consumers have access to affordable everyday essentials.

According to the company, maintaining both a competitive food market and a resilient domestic food system is important for Canadian consumers and the broader economy.

data.title: How Starlink Limits Force Ukraine to Fight With the Brakes On — WSJ
data.description:
By Ian Lovett, Ievgeniia Sivorka and Alistair MacDonald

Early on a recent morning, Ukrainian officer Vladyslav Oliinyk ordered his drone team to hit a Russian armored vehicle spotted on a road in southeastern Ukraine.

The drones disabled the vehicle and set upon some Russian infantrymen, he said. But the Ukrainian pilots had to take care to fly slowly, or risk losing the connection — because of recently imposed speed limits on Starshield, a military-grade version of the satellite internet service Starlink.

Ukraine's military relies on Starshield — a subscription service provided by Elon Musk's SpaceX under U.S. government contracts — to disrupt Russian army logistics, and to help intercept jet-powered Russian drones that are pounding Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities.

For two periods this fall, Ukrainian units say they have encountered speed limits of 100 miles an hour on their Starshield terminals. At that speed, battlefield drones are easier for the Russians to shoot down — and interceptor drones have little chance of catching Russian jet-powered drones.

Ukraine's short-range drones, which counter Russia's invasion forces near the front line, are mostly radio-controlled, while some use fiber-optic cables.

But Ukraine is heavily dependent on Starshield for its midrange drone operations against Russian forces' rear areas and supply lines. The midrange campaign has played a major role in limiting Russia to tiny territorial gains this year.

Musk first ordered speed limits on Starshield in October amid political tensions between President Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. After a backlash, including from U.S. lawmakers, Trump asked Musk to restore the satellite service.

But since Nov. 10, Ukrainian drone units say they have again faced a 100 mph speed cap over Russian-occupied areas of Ukraine. Kyiv and its supporters have renewed their protests, but the limits have stayed in place.

Neither SpaceX nor the U.S. government has admitted responsibility. Musk said last week that his Starlink satellites, which Ukraine's Starshield service uses, aren't meant for drone strikes that kill people.

Starlink's more widely used commercial service has had a much lower speed cap in Ukraine since early 2026, effectively limiting its use by Ukraine's military to static purposes such as communication between troops. Starlink and Starshield don't work over Russian territory, where Ukraine uses other methods to steer its drone strikes against arms factories, refineries and other targets.

Kyiv is worried that the speed cap in Russian-held parts of Ukraine is a new reality that could hurt the effectiveness of its midrange strike campaign. Over time, that could help Moscow to better move troops, ammunition and other supplies to the front line, enabling Russian offensives next year, military analysts warn.

Most midrange drone pilots have little choice but to try to live with Starshield's new limits — even if it means they can't work as effectively as a few months ago.

"Since they capped the speed, there are some missions we can't do, including missile interceptions," said Oliinyk, a senior lieutenant with the First Unmanned Systems Battalion of Ukraine's First Separate Assault Regiment.

Slower-flying drones can still hit Russian armored vehicles or supply trucks. But to reach their target, they must first get through Russian air defenses. "With lower speeds, our drones are easier to intercept," Oliinyk said.

It often takes more drones now to hit a given target, because many more of them are being lost to connection failures or Russian fire, said a midrange drone pilot known by his call sign Loza.

"What you see is a gradual loss of efficiency. Fewer opportunities. More work for the same result," he said.

The speed restrictions can appear random sometimes, several drone operators said. At times, they can hit speeds of up to 125 mph over Russian-occupied areas. At other times, the connection cuts out even at low speeds.

"We don't really know what to expect," Loza said. "Things seem fine, and then suddenly you're dealing with connection problems."

Loza and other operators expressed frustration at having to rely on a technology that Ukraine can't control.

"You can have good equipment, experienced people, everything ready to go, and still find yourself unable to do what you need to do," said a communications officer working in the southern Zaporizhzhia region, known by his call sign Shtanga.

Ukrainian forces are looking for alternatives to SpaceX's satellites. At times, drone pilots are using mesh networks, which use drones to relay radio signals to other drones, or cellular networks. Some drone teams are using HiSKY, an Israeli satellite-communications provider, according to two people familiar with the matter.

But those options all come with significant downsides. Cellular networks only work in some areas, and those connections are easier for Russians to jam. Mesh networks require expensive equipment, and the video feeds often have significant time lags.

European satellite providers such as Eutelsat's OneWeb have far smaller networks than Starlink, and their terminals are more expensive.

"At present, we do not have a fully viable alternative to replace Starlink," said Dmytro Batekha, founder of Ukrainian military analysis group Oko Hora. "There are some European systems, but their deployment is on a very limited scale."

In addition, many of the drones Ukraine is making are configured for SpaceX's services. Reconfiguring them to work on other communications systems often requires sending them back to the manufacturer.

Some of the Ukrainian munitions used to attack the bridge connecting occupied Crimea to Russia used HiSKY, according to people familiar with the matter. Unlike Starlink, HiSKY also works inside Russia, and Ukrainian drone teams have used it to hunt for Russian ballistic-missile launchers, one of these people said.

HiSKY didn't respond to requests for comment.

The Israeli system requires more technical expertise, including having specialists present during missions, compared with easy-to-use Starlink terminals, this person said. That means it is only likely to be used for particularly high-value missions, rather than routine drone missions that Ukrainian forces need to launch every day while Russia maintains its invasion.

data.title: DPC Dash - Domino's Pizza China Wins Sixth Seven-Star Award, Underscoring Its Quality Control Advantage and Sustainable Operating Efficiency as It Expands
data.description:
HONG KONG, Nov. 28, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- DPC Dash – Domino's Pizza China ("DPC Dash" or the "Company") (1405.HK), Domino's Pizza's exclusive master franchisee in the Chinese Mainland, the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region of China, and the Macau Special Administrative Region of China, received its sixth Seven-Star Award at the 15th Annual Seven-Star Awards for Outstanding Contributions in Food Safety & Public Health, held in Shanghai on November 26. Winning the award six years in a row, while rapidly expanding its store network, reflects DPC Dash's sustained work on food safety governance, supply chain standardization and measurable ESG practices. For investors, the award provides independent recognition of the Company's ability to maintain quality controls and operational consistency as it scales.

Strong food safety and quality governance gives DPC Dash a competitive advantage, helping protect its brand and replicate its store operating model as it expands rapidly. As of September 30, 2026, the Company operated 1,634 stores across 87 cities in the Chinese Mainland, up 24% from the end of 2025, and its fully company-operated model gives it direct oversight across the network. The Company applies a rigorous farm-to-table food safety framework, from ingredient sourcing to in-store customer service, using standardized procedures, digital controls and training for all employees. These measures help manage operational and reputational risks, maintain product consistency and encourage repeat visits as DPC Dash enters new cities and expands in existing markets.

DPC Dash invests in centralized supply chain infrastructure ahead of store expansion to maintain consistent quality across regions and capture economies of scale. By the end of 2025, all (100%) of the Company's central kitchens then in operation had passed third-party audits under the internationally recognized FSSC 22000 food safety management system certification scheme, aligning with the quality and compliance standards that international institutions look for. On August 21, 2026, DPC Dash opened its fourth supply chain center in Wuhan, which combines production, warehousing and distribution and can support more than 200 stores. An integrated digital platform manages procurement, warehousing and distribution, and monitors cold-chain shipments around the clock from production to store delivery. As store density increases in the region, the hub helps make order fulfillment across regions more efficient and improve the supply chain cost structure, while supporting consistent quality standards in new and expanding markets. This supports the Company's nationwide expansion over the medium to long term.

DPC Dash builds sustainability into its efforts to lower costs and improve efficiency across its stores and supply chain. Its priorities include using energy and resources more efficiently, reducing food waste and adopting sustainable packaging. In its 2025 Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) Report, the Company disclosed that sustainable packaging accounted for 85.13% of packaging used. All snack boxes and pizza trays are made from recyclable materials, and delivery and dine-in cutlery is made from biodegradable materials. The Company also fits store ovens with energy-saving shields that recover waste heat. This reduces heat loss, directly improves store-level energy efficiency and lowers the Company's environmental footprint, supporting long-term profitability and sustainable growth.

Initiated by the Seven-Star Convention Alliance, the Seven-Star Awards are an established industry benchmark promoting food safety, public health and sustainable development. The awards assess companies across seven criteria: organizational structure, supply chain management, production standards, corporate integrity, health advocacy, innovation leadership and sustainable development. Looking ahead, DPC Dash will continue to strengthen food safety governance and its centralized supply chain as it expands its store network nationwide, focusing on consistent product quality, operational efficiency and transparent ESG disclosure. The Company will also continue to combine global product ideas with Chinese consumers' preferences to broaden its localized pizza menu, drive long-term growth and create sustainable long-term value for shareholders.

DPC Dash is Domino's Pizza's exclusive master franchisee in the Chinese Mainland, the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region of China and the Macau Special Administrative Region of China. Domino's Pizza, Inc., DPC Dash's global franchisor, is one of the most widely-recognized global consumer brands and the world's largest pizza company. Led by a seasoned and visionary management team, DPC Dash is a market leader that differentiates from competitors with, among others, a continually innovated and localized pizza-focused menu, unique expertise and leadership in delivery, technology focus and scalable and replicable store economic model. As of September 30, 2026, DPC Dash operated 1,634 stores in 87 cities in the Chinese Mainland.

data.title: Citigroup's $35 Billion Bookkeeping Snafu Sparks Shake-Up in Upper Ranks — WSJ
data.description:
By Alexander Saeedy, Ben Dummett and Joe Wallace

A $35 billion bookkeeping blunder in Citigroup's London hub has sparked an internal shake-up and undermined efforts by America's most error-prone big bank to repair its relationship with regulators around the world.

The bank over the summer injected approximately $3 billion into a major U.K. subsidiary after an employee revealed it had been undercounting a key measure of its balance sheet, said a spokeswoman, who described the error as an "internal capital modeling issue."

The mistake shaved $35 billion off the unit's "risk-weighted assets," which regulators use to determine how much loss-absorbing capital banks need to hold. The broker-dealer subsidiary is one of Citi's biggest and most important outside the U.S.

Citi is now scrambling to limit the damage. At least two managing directors who had oversight of financial reports to regulators are no longer in their positions as of this fall, people familiar with the matter said. The bank declined to comment on their departure.

The bank's chief risk officer, Zdenek Turek, recently moved to London from New York and is working to correct the reporting issues, some of the people said. A spokeswoman said Turek's move to London was planned before the problem came to light, adding that the subsidiary never fell below minimum capital levels required by regulators.

Tiina Lee, Citi's chief executive in the U.K., said she was stepping down in October. A spokeswoman said her departure was unconnected to the reporting problem, but her exit adds to the turbulence in Citi's large London operation.

"This past summer, Citi learned that a capital model used by a European trading subsidiary was applied to one location where the model didn't have regulatory approval," Citi's spokeswoman said in a statement. "Citi completed remedial actions and injected capital to immediately restore the subsidiary's buffers. This issue had no impact on our overall capital levels...or our financial performance."

The mistake is a setback for CEO Jane Fraser's attempt to draw a line under Citi's long history of unforced errors, some of which contributed to the ouster of her predecessor. The bank is still working to fix internal controls after a slapdown by U.S. regulators in 2020. That year, Citi accidentally paid $900 million to creditors of a cosmetic company.

In 2022, a Citi trader sparked a brief crash in European stocks by entering a preposterously large number in a trading system, and in 2024, U.S. regulators fined the bank $136 million for failing to make progress on cleaning up its act.

Citi has discussed the accounting problem at its U.K.-based unit with officials from the Federal Reserve, which supervises the global parent company, people familiar with the matter said. The spokeswoman declined to comment on conversations with regulators.

The problem for Citi concerns the use of proprietary financial models to calculate "risk-weighted assets," a measure that requires banks to hold more capital against assets — such as complex derivatives — that are riskier than others, such as government bonds. Some banks are allowed to use their own models to determine how much risk they have taken and the requisite capital they should hold to protect from losses.

While the U.K. regulator had given Citi the go-ahead to use some of their own proprietary models, the bank applied them beyond the scope of that approval.

The spokeswoman said the Bank of England hadn't given the green light for a Europe-based desk to use the internal models, which deployed them nonetheless.

The models undercounted Citi's actual risk-taking by around $35 billion, or around 20% of all the reported risk-weighted assets at Citigroup's U.K. subsidiary. The U.K. unit reported it had around $150 billion in risk-weighted assets last year, according to corporate filings.

Calculating risk-weighted assets is inherently complex, so errors aren't unusual. But Citi's mistake stands out for its magnitude, according to one of the people familiar with the matter.

The problem came to light after an employee rang the alarm. The bank then "quickly commenced an internal investigation and escalated this issue to regulators," the Citi spokeswoman said.

The parent company had the funds available to send capital to London and didn't have to sell stock or borrow to do so, the spokeswoman said.

A U.K. regulatory filing shows that at the start of November, Manjira Sen-Gosain, Citigroup's chief risk officer for its U.K. unit, left her position. Her LinkedIn page has been taken down.

Sen-Gosain couldn't be reached for comment.

Banks require approval from the Bank of England, which regulates banks in the U.K., before being allowed to use their own internal models to calculate risk-weighted assets. Persuading the central bank can be arduous — particularly if the model is going to be applied to a significant part of the bank's business. Risk-weighted asset models can permit significant reductions in capital requirements.

Once they are in use, the models typically have some element of self-testing. Bank of England supervisors often keep a close eye on how they are performing to make sure banks aren't undercounting, according to people familiar with the process.

It isn't uncommon for the Bank of England to approve models for certain defined purposes. Going beyond the limits of the approval can be seen as a big problem by the regulator, though how serious depends on the size of the ultimate mistake.

data.title: Glass Lewis backs Vail Resorts board in proxy fight with activist Oasis
data.description:
Key points:
  • Glass Lewis backs nine Vail directors before December 14 vote
  • Oasis seeks to elect Bob Chapek, Ashton Hudson to board
  • Glass Lewis raised concerns about Chapek's financial arrangement with Oasis

By Svea Herbst-Bayliss

Proxy advisory firm Glass Lewis urged Vail Resorts investors to reelect the mountain resort operator's directors, arguing the three dissident candidates are not qualified to sit on the board or are too financially tied to hedge fund Oasis Management.

Glass Lewis, one of the two leading US firms that guide investor voting on issues such as board elections ‌and ​corporate mergers, backed the company's nine directors in one of the season's most hotly contested fights before the December 14 vote. The Glass Lewis report was seen by Reuters on Friday.

Proxy advisory firm Egan-Jones earlier recommended investors elect all of Vail's director candidates. Institutional Shareholder Services, the biggest proxy advisory firm, has not yet issued its recommendation.

Oasis Management, Vail's fourth-largest investor with a 9.6% stake, is urging investors to elect its two proposed directors, former Walt Disney CEO Bob Chapek and Ashton Hudson, who has served on various boards.

Gregory Meyer, an independent shareholder, wants shareholders to elect him to the board. Both Oasis and Meyer have criticized the company's financial performance and stock price, which has tumbled more than 57% in the last five years, even though it has gained 7% since January. Vail's stock closed at $143.07 on Friday, leaving it with a market value of $5.1 billion.

"Coming off a weather-wracked fiscal year punctuated by the sudden return of (CEO Rob) Katz, Vail has bolstered its board and executive bench and launched a series of tactical initiatives which appear closely tuned to both the Company's legacy failings and investor feedback derived from extended engagement," Glass Lewis wrote.

The report criticized the dissident candidates. "The establishment of singular compensatory arrangements with Mr. Chapek, a nominee intended to be independent of Oasis — runs counter to sound governance," the report said.

Glass Lewis cited Oasis' compensation to Chapek, saying it was structured "in exceptionally atypical fashion." Oasis said in a regulatory filing in October that it is paying Chapek $100,000 per month in consulting fees and extending a $500,000 forgivable loan, to be used to purchase Vail common stock if Chapek is elected.

"The remaining nominees — M. Ashton Hudson on the one hand, Gregory Meyer on the other — do not clearly offer experience and expertise more effectively aligned with Vail's current strategic trajectory," the report said.

Meyer, who has bought Vail's multi-resort Epic season pass for 12 consecutive seasons, said on Friday he was concerned about the rising cost of tickets and a falling stock price.

"Shareholders are getting less and skiers are paying more," Meyer told Reuters. "That isn't a strategy working. It's a board that needs fresh perspective, and I'm asking shareholders to give it one on December 14."

Oasis was not immediately available for comment.
